Welcome to Statistics
Welcome to Statistics at Frederick Douglass High School!
Statistics is the math of data. Every day, people use numbers to tell you something. An ad says “average pay is \(\$80{,}000\).” A news story says “most people agree.” Statistics helps you check if those numbers tell the truth.

1.1.2 - Dot Plots
A dot plot puts the values on a number line. Each value gets one dot. Dots for the same value stack up.
This dot plot shows the same siblings data:





The height of each stack is the frequency. The stack above 1 is the tallest, so 1 is the most common.

Count the dots above 2, 3, and 4: \(3 + 1 + 1 = 5\) students.





1.1.3 - Histograms
A histogram is a bar graph for number data. The values are put into groups called bins. Each bar is one bin.





The tallest bar is 170 to 180. So 7 students are from 170 cm to 180 cm tall.
There are no gaps between the bars. The bins touch, like the numbers on a number line.

If a value is on a line between two bars, it goes in the bar on the right.
160 goes in the 160 to 170 bar.


The graph shows that 6 students are from 160 cm to 170 cm. It does not show their exact heights. A dot plot shows every value. A histogram does not.


When there is a lot of data, or the values are spread out.
Heights in centimeters can be 158, 163, 171, 179, and so on. A dot plot would have many short stacks. A histogram groups them, so the shape is easy to see.

title: 1.2 - Mean, Median, and Shape
text:
👥 Learn Together
A small company puts this in a job ad:
Four of the five people there earn less than \(\$40{,}000\). How can the ad be true?
In this lesson, you learn two ways to find the center of data: the mean and the median. You also learn how the shape of a graph can make them different.

title: 1.2 - Mean, Median, and Shape
text:
1.2.1 - The Mean
The mean is also called the average.


Add all the values.
Divide by how many values there are.


Example 1: 2, 3, 8, 3, 4
\[
2 + 3 + 8 + 3 + 4 = 20
\]
There are 5 values.
\[
20 \div 5 = 4
\]
The mean is 4.

\[
\bar{x} = \frac{\Sigma x}{n}
\]

\(\Sigma\) is the Greek capital letter sigma. It means add up.
\(\Sigma x\) means add up all the values.
\(\bar{x}\) (“x-bar”) is the mean.
\(n\) is how many values there are.

For the example: \(\Sigma x = 20\) and \(n = 5\), so \(\bar{x} = \frac{20}{5} = 4\).




1.2.2 - The Median
The median is the middle value.


Put the values in order.
Find the middle value.


Example 2: the same data, 2, 3, 8, 3, 4
In order: 2, 3, 3, 4, 8
The middle value is 3. So the median is 3.
Example 3: an even number of values, 2, 3, 5, 8
There are two numbers in the middle: 3 and 5. The median is the number halfway between them.
\[
(3 + 5) \div 2 = 4
\]
The median is 4.

Mean: \(6 + 1 + 9 + 4 = 20\). Then \(20 \div 4 = 5\). The mean is 5.
Median: In order: 1, 4, 6, 9. Then \((4 + 6) \div 2 = 5\). The median is 5.


The mode is the value that happens most often. In 2, 3, 8, 3, 4, the mode is 3.




1.2.3 - Shape Changes the Mean
The tail is the long, low side of a graph.

The mean is pulled toward the tail. The median is not pulled much.









Shape
What it looks like
Mean and median




Skewed left
Tail on the left
mean < median


Symmetric
Both sides match
mean ≈ median


Skewed right
Tail on the right
mean > median




The pay is 30,000, 32,000, 35,000, 38,000, and 265,000 dollars.
The mean is \(400{,}000 \div 5 = 80{,}000\) dollars. The owner’s pay is a long tail on the right. It pulls the mean up.
The median is 35,000 dollars. That is a better description of a typical worker.




1.2.4 - Real Example: US Household Income
Most households earn a medium amount. A small number of households earn millions of dollars. That makes a long tail on the right.







Median: about \(\$84{,}000\)
Mean: about \(\$121{,}000\)

Half of households earn less than the median. Most households earn less than the mean.
When you hear “the average household,” ask: is that the mean or the median?
Source: US Census Bureau, Income in the United States: 2024. Median \(\$83{,}730\). Mean about \(\$121{,}000\).

title: 1.3 - Quartiles, IQR, and Box Plots
text:
👥 Learn Together
The median cuts data into two halves. What if you cut each half in half again?
You get four parts. Each part has about 25% of the data. The numbers that make those cuts are called quartiles.
In this lesson, you find quartiles, use them to measure spread, and draw a box plot.

title: 1.3 - Quartiles, IQR, and Box Plots
text:
1.3.1 - Finding Quartiles


Put the data in order.
Find the median. It splits the data into a lower half and an upper half.
Q1 = the median of the lower half.
Q3 = the median of the upper half.

Odd number of values? Leave the median out of both halves.

Example 1: an odd number of values (11)
3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15, 18, 20
The median is 10. Leave it out of the halves.



Lower half
Upper half




3, 4, 6, 7, 9
12, 13, 15, 18, 20


Q1 = 6
Q3 = 15



Example 2: an even number of values (10)
1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 14, 18
There are two middle values, 7 and 9. The median is \((7 + 9) \div 2 = 8\).



Lower half
Upper half




1, 3, 4, 6, 7
9, 10, 12, 14, 18


Q1 = 4
Q3 = 12






1.3.2 - The Five-Number Summary and the IQR
The five-number summary is five numbers:
minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum
The interquartile range (IQR) shows how spread out the middle half of the data is.
\[
\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1
\]
\(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) are another way to write Q1 and Q3.
For Example 1: IQR \(= 15 - 6 = 9\).
For Example 2: IQR \(= 12 - 4 = 8\).

7, 15, 2, 10, 4, 11, 6


In order: 2, 4, 6, 7, 10, 11, 15. The median is 7.
Lower half: 2, 4, 6. So Q1 = 4.
Upper half: 10, 11, 15. So Q3 = 11.
Five-number summary: 2, 4, 7, 11, 15. IQR \(= 11 - 4 = 7\).




1.3.3 - Box Plots
A box plot draws the five-number summary on a number line. Here is Example 1.






The box goes from Q1 to Q3. Its length is the IQR.
The line inside the box is the median.
The whiskers go out to the minimum and the maximum.


The 4 parts have the same number of values, not the same width. A short part means the values are packed close together. A long part means they are spread out.


Range \(=\) maximum \(-\) minimum. One extreme value changes it a lot.
The IQR only uses the middle half of the data. One extreme value does not move it much. The median works the same way: one extreme value moves the mean a lot, but not the median.

text:
👥 Learn Together
Nine students ride the bus to school. Eight of them ride from 12 to 22 minutes. One student rides 45 minutes.
Is 45 just a long ride, or is it far away from the rest? Statistics has a rule to decide.
In this lesson, you read box plots, compare two box plots, and find outliers.

1.4.1 - Reading a Box Plot

The left whisker (52 to 68) is the longest part. It still holds only about 25% of the students. A long part means those scores are spread out.




1.4.2 - Comparing Box Plots
Put both box plots on the same number line. Then compare the centers and the spreads.

The afternoon class scored higher (larger median). The afternoon scores are also closer together (smaller IQR).



1.4.3 - Outliers
An outlier is a value far away from the rest of the data.


Find Q1, Q3, and the IQR.
Lower fence \(= Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\)
Upper fence \(= Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\)
A value below the lower fence or above the upper fence is an outlier.


Example: 3, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 30
Q1 = 8.5, Q3 = 13.5, and IQR = 5.
\[
1.5 \times 5 = 7.5
\]
\[
\text{Lower fence} = 8.5 - 7.5 = 1 \qquad \text{Upper fence} = 13.5 + 7.5 = 21
\]
30 is above 21, so 30 is an outlier. 3 is not below 1, so 3 is not an outlier.





On a box plot, an outlier is a dot. The whisker stops at the last value that is not an outlier. Here, that is 14.

Q1 = 20, Q3 = 30. Is 48 an outlier?


IQR \(= 30 - 20 = 10\). Upper fence \(= 30 + 1.5 \times 10 = 30 + 15 = 45\).
48 is above 45, so 48 is an outlier.

title: 2.3 - Percentiles and Z-Scores
text:
👥 Learn Together
You scored 85 on a test. Is that good?
If everyone else scored 95, it is not so good. If everyone else scored 60, it is great. A score only has meaning when you compare it to the rest of the data.
In this lesson, you use percentiles and z-scores to tell where one value stands.

title: 2.3 - Percentiles and Z-Scores
text:
2.3.1 - Percentiles

The percentile of a value is the percent of the data that is below it.
\[
\text{percentile} = \frac{\text{number of values below}}{\text{total number of values}} \times 100
\]

Example: 20 students took a test. 15 students scored below 85.
\[
15 \div 20 = 0.75
\]
A score of 85 is at the 75th percentile. It is higher than 75% of the class.

Scoring at the 75th percentile does not mean you got 75% of the questions right. It means you scored higher than 75% of the people.




2.3.2 - Z-Scores

A z-score tells how many standard deviations a value is above or below the mean.
\[
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}
\]

\(x\) is the value.
\(\mu\) (the Greek letter mu) is the mean.
\(\sigma\) (a small sigma) is the standard deviation. Do not mix it up with the capital \(\Sigma\), which means add up.
\(z > 0\): above the mean
\(z < 0\): below the mean
\(z = 0\): equal to the mean


Example: A test has a mean of 70 and an SD of 10. What is the z-score of 85?
\[
z = \frac{85 - 70}{10} = \frac{15}{10} = 1.5
\]
85 is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.






\[
z = \frac{55 - 70}{10} = \frac{-15}{10} = -1.5
\]
55 is 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.

Z-scores let you compare values from different data sets.

What it is
Example




Marginal distribution
Percents from the totals (the margins). Divide by the grand total.
Job: \(\frac{20}{60} \approx 33\%\). No job: \(\frac{40}{60} \approx 67\%\).


Conditional distribution
Percents inside one group. Divide by that group’s total.
Students who play a sport. Job: \(\frac{8}{30} \approx 27\%\). No job: \(\frac{22}{30} \approx 73\%\).




“Of the students who play a sport, what percent have a job?”

Sport: about 27% have a job.

Conditional percents are about the same: there is no association.



We cannot tell from this table. An association only says the two things happen together. It does not prove cause. Maybe practice takes time away from a job. Maybe something else explains both. You will learn more about cause in Unit 5.

title: 4.1 - Scatterplots and Lines of Best Fit
text:
4.1.1 - Describing a Scatterplot
A scatterplot shows two numbers for each person or thing. The first number (\(x\)) goes across. The second number (\(y\)) goes up.









Ask
The study data




Direction
As \(x\) goes up, does \(y\) go up (positive) or down (negative)? No pattern at all is no association.
Positive


Form
Do the dots follow a line (linear) or a curve?
Linear


Strength
Are the dots close to a line (strong), a little spread out (moderate), or very spread out (weak)?
Strong


Unusual
Any outliers or clusters?
None






4.1.2 - The Line of Best Fit
A line of best fit follows the trend of the dots.

It goes through the middle of the dots.
About the same number of dots are above it as below it.






Finding its equation. Pick two points on the line. They do not have to be dots: \((2, 64)\) and \((6, 84)\).
Slope (\(m\)):
\[
m = \frac{84 - 64}{6 - 2} = \frac{20}{4} = 5
\]
y-intercept (\(b\)):
\[
64 = 5(2) + b \quad \Rightarrow \quad b = 54
\]
Equation:
\[
\hat{y} = 5x + 54
\]

\(\hat{y}\) is read “y-hat.” The hat means predicted. The line predicts \(y\). It does not give the exact \(y\) for every student.




4.1.3 - Predicting
A student studies 5 hours:
\[
\hat{y} = 5(5) + 54 = 79
\]
The predicted score is 79.

Predicting far outside the data is called extrapolation. It is risky.
12 hours gives \(\hat{y} = 5(12) + 54 = 114\). A test score cannot be more than 100. The data only goes from 1 to 8 hours.


\(\hat{y} = 5(7) + 54 = 35 + 54 = 89\)

Does ice cream cause sunburns? Of course not. In this lesson, you learn what a line of best fit tells you. You measure how strong a pattern is. You also learn why a pattern does not prove a cause.

title: 4.2 - Slope, Intercept, and Correlation
text:
4.2.1 - Slope and Intercept in Context
A student measured a plant every week. The line of best fit is \(\hat{y} = 2.5x + 4\).













Meaning




Slope (2.5)
For each additional week, the predicted height increases by 2.5 cm.


y-intercept (4)
When \(x = 0\) (the day it was planted), the predicted height is 4 cm.




Slope: For each additional [\(x\) unit], the predicted [\(y\)] increases (or decreases) by [slope and units].
Intercept: When [\(x\)] is 0, the predicted [\(y\)] is [intercept and units].


If \(x\) is a person’s height, then \(x = 0\) is not possible. The intercept is only there to place the line.




4.2.2 - The Correlation Coefficient
The correlation coefficient \(r\) measures how strong a linear pattern is.







\(r\) is always from \(-1\) to \(1\).
The sign shows the direction: \(r > 0\) is positive, \(r < 0\) is negative.
The size shows the strength: close to \(1\) or \(-1\) is strong. Close to \(0\) is weak.



\(r = -0.8\). It is closer to \(-1\) than \(0.6\) is to \(1\). The minus sign only tells the direction.




4.2.3 - Correlation Is Not Causation
Ice cream sales and sunburns have a strong positive correlation. But ice cream does not cause sunburns. Hot, sunny weather causes both.
A hidden cause like this is called a lurking variable.

A correlation shows that two things change together. It does not prove that one causes the other.

\[

\]

Square every residual and add them up:
\[

\]
The least-squares regression line is the line that makes this sum as small as possible. Calculators and computers find this line for you.

title: 5.1 - Samples, Studies, and Bias
text:
👥 Learn Together
A radio station asks listeners to call in: Should school start later? 90% of the callers say yes.
Does that mean 90% of all students agree? Not necessarily. The people who called in chose to call. They may care much more than other students.
In this lesson, you learn who is in a study, what kind of study it is, and how bias can make the results wrong.

title: 5.1 - Samples, Studies, and Bias
text:
5.1.1 - Population and Sample









Meaning
Example




Population
The whole group we want to learn about.
All 1,200 students at a school.


Sample
The part of the population we collect data from.
100 of those students.



We can only generalize (say the results are true for the whole population) if the sample represents the population well.



5.1.2 - Three Types of Studies








Type
What happens
Example




Sample survey
Ask a sample questions.
Ask 100 students how many hours they sleep.


Observational study
Watch or measure. Do not change anything.
Compare the grades of students who do and do not play sports.


Experiment
Do something to the subjects (a treatment) and measure what happens.
Give half the students a 10-minute break before a test. Compare scores.




An observational study. The scientist measures, but does not tell anyone how much soda to drink.




5.1.3 - Bias
Bias is when the way we collect data favors some answers. A biased sample does not represent the population.








Type of bias
What happens
Example




Voluntary response
People choose if they answer. People with strong feelings answer most.
The radio call-in poll.


Convenience
The sample is whoever is easy to reach.
Asking only your friends.


Undercoverage
Some groups are left out of the sample.
Calling only home phones. Many people do not have one.


Nonresponse
People who were chosen do not answer.
Half of the mailed surveys never come back.


Response
The question or the setting pushes people to answer a certain way.
“Don’t you agree that our great principal deserves a raise?”




A call-in poll with 10,000 callers is still biased. More callers do not fix the problem. The callers still chose to call.

title: 5.2 - Sampling Methods
text:
5.2.1 - Five Ways to Choose a Sample








Method
How it works
Example (60 of 1,200)




Simple random sample (SRS)
Every group of the same size has the same chance of being chosen. Like drawing names from a hat.
Number the students 1 to 1,200. A random number generator picks 60 numbers.


Stratified
Split the population into groups (strata). People in the same group are alike in some way. Take a random sample from each group.
Randomly pick 15 students from each grade: 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th.


Cluster
Split the population into groups (clusters). Randomly pick some whole groups.
Randomly pick 3 homerooms. Ask everyone in them.


Systematic
Pick a random start. Then take every \(k\)th person. \(k\) is the population size divided by the sample size.
Start at a random student from 1 to 20. Then take every 20th student on the list.


Convenience (bad)
Take whoever is easy to reach.
Ask the first 60 students who walk in the door.





Stratified: a few from every group.
Cluster: everyone from a few groups.



\(k = 1{,}200 \div 80 = 15\).
Pick a random start from 1 to 15. Then take every 15th student on the list.

title: 5.3 - Experiments
text:
👥 Learn Together
Does a new pill stop headaches? You could compare people who chose to take it with people who did not. But those two groups might be different in many ways: age, sleep, stress.
An experiment solves this. The researcher gives the treatment on purpose and compares groups that are alike.

title: 5.3 - Experiments
text:
5.3.1 - The Language of Experiments



Word
In the headache experiment




Subjects (experimental units)
The 40 volunteers with headaches


Explanatory variable
What we change: the type of pill


Treatments
The things we compare: new pill, placebo


Response variable
What we measure: headache relief


Control group
The group that does not get the new treatment


Placebo
A fake treatment that looks real, like a sugar pill


Double-blind
Neither the subjects nor the people measuring know who got which pill








This is a completely randomized design. Chance alone decides which group each subject joins.



5.3.2 - Principles of a Good Experiment


Control: Compare to a control group. Keep everything else the same for both groups.
Random assignment: Use chance to put subjects into groups. Then the groups are about the same, except for the treatment.
Replication: Use many subjects. With more subjects, chance differences between the groups get smaller.



People often feel better just because they think they got medicine. This is the placebo effect. With a placebo, both groups think they are being treated. So any extra difference comes from the real pill.




5.3.3 - Matched Pairs and Blocks
In a matched pairs design, each subject gets both treatments, in a random order. Or you pair up very similar subjects, like twins. Each twin gets a different treatment.
Example: Which running shoe is faster? Each runner runs once in each shoe. A coin flip decides which shoe goes first. Comparing each runner to themselves removes the differences between runners.

Runners might be tired on the second run, or warmed up. The coin keeps that from always helping the same shoe.

Randomized block design: first split the subjects into groups that are alike (blocks), like boys and girls. Then randomly assign the treatments inside each block. Comparing inside each block keeps the differences between blocks out of the result.

title: 5.4 - What a Study Can Prove
text:
5.4.1 - Two Questions


Was the sample chosen at random from the population? If yes, we can generalize to the population.
Were the treatments given by random assignment? If yes, and the difference is too big to be just chance, we can say the treatment caused the result.











Random assignment
No random assignment




Random sample
Cause: yes. Generalize: yes.
Cause: no. Generalize: yes.


Not a random sample

Repeat 100 times.

title: 6.1 - Venn Diagrams and the Addition Rule
text:
6.1.1 - Probability
Probability is how likely something is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). When every outcome is equally likely:
\[
P(A) = \frac{\text{number of ways } A \text{ can happen}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}
\]

\(P(A)\) is read “the probability of \(A\).”
Complement: \(P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)\). Some books write \(P(A^C)\).

Example: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue marbles. Pick one. \(P(\text{red}) = \frac{3}{10}\), and \(P(\text{not red}) = 1 - \frac{3}{10} = \frac{7}{10}\).



6.1.2 - “Or” and “And”









Symbol
Read it as
Meaning




\(A \cup B\)
“\(A\) union \(B\)” or “\(A\) or \(B\)”
\(A\) happens, or \(B\) happens, or both


\(A \cap B\)
“\(A\) intersect \(B\)” or “\(A\) and \(B\)”
\(A\) and \(B\) both happen (the overlap)









If we add \(12 + 10\), the 4 students who play both are counted twice. Subtract them once:
\[
P(S \cup B) = \frac{12}{30} + \frac{10}{30} - \frac{4}{30} = \frac{18}{30} = 0.6
\]

\[
P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
\]




6.1.3 - Mutually Exclusive Events
Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen. Then \(P(A \cap B) = 0\), so
\[
P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)
\]
Example: Roll a number cube. Rolling a 1 and rolling a 2 cannot both happen. \(P(1 \cup 2) = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{3}\).

A standard deck has 52 cards: 4 suits (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades), with 13 cards in each suit (A, 2 to 10, J, Q, K).


They are not mutually exclusive: the queen of hearts and the queen of diamonds are both.
\[
\frac{26}{52} + \frac{4}{52} - \frac{2}{52} = \frac{28}{52} = \frac{7}{13}
\]

title: 6.2 - The Multiplication Rule
text:
👥 Learn Together
You guess on 3 multiple-choice questions. Each question has 4 choices. What is the probability you get all 3 right?
Each guess has a \(\frac{1}{4}\) chance. The questions do not affect each other, so you multiply:
\[
P(\text{all 3 right}) = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{64}
\]
That is about a 1.6% chance. In this lesson, you learn when and how to multiply probabilities.

title: 6.2 - The Multiplication Rule
text:
6.2.1 - Independent Events
Two events are independent if one happening does not change the probability of the other.

\[
P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)
\]

Example: Flip a coin and roll a number cube.
\[
P(\text{heads} \cap 6) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12}
\]



6.2.2 - Dependent Events
Two events are dependent if one happening changes the probability of the other.
A bag has 5 red and 3 blue marbles. Draw 2 marbles.



With replacement (put the first one back)
Without replacement (keep the first one out)




The second draw is the same as the first. Independent.
The bag changes: 4 red and 3 blue are left. Dependent.


\(P(\text{red, red}) = \frac{5}{8} \cdot \frac{5}{8} = \frac{25}{64}\)
\(P(\text{red, red}) = \frac{5}{8} \cdot \frac{4}{7} = \frac{20}{56} = \frac{5}{14}\)




\[
P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A)
\]
\(P(B \mid A)\) is read “the probability of \(B\) given \(A\).” It is the probability of \(B\) after \(A\) has already happened. The bar \(\mid\) means “given.”

In the marble example, \(P(\text{red second} \mid \text{red first}) = \frac{4}{7}\).



6.2.3 - “At Least One”
“At least one” questions are often easier with the complement:
\[
P(\text{at least one wrong}) = 1 - P(\text{all right})
\]

\(P(\text{all right}) = \frac{1}{64}\), so \(P(\text{at least one wrong}) = 1 - \frac{1}{64} = \frac{63}{64}\).

6.1 - Add for “Or”

\[
P(M \cup A) = P(M) + P(A) - P(M \cap A) = \frac{8}{20} + \frac{6}{20} - \frac{3}{20} = \frac{11}{20} = 0.55

\[

Flip a coin 2 times and count the heads. You might get 0, 1, or 2 heads. Are they all equally likely?

title: 7.2 - Expected Value
text:
👥 Learn Together
A soccer team scores 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4 goals in a game. Each number of goals has its own probability. How many goals does the team score on average?
You cannot just average 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. Some values happen more often than others. In this lesson, you find the expected value, an average that uses the probabilities. Then you use probability to decide what is fair.

title: Glossary
text:
addition rule
\(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\). Subtract the overlap because it was counted twice.
See Also: mutually exclusive



association
Two variables are associated when knowing one tells you something about the other. In a two-way table, the conditional percents are different from group to group. An association does not prove that one thing causes the other.
See Also: conditional distribution



bias
When the way data is collected favors some answers over others. A biased sample does not represent the population.

Example:
Voluntary response, convenience, undercoverage, nonresponse, and response bias.




bin
One group of values in a histogram. Each bar of a histogram is one bin.

Example:
The bin “10 to 20” holds every value from 10 up to (but not including) 20.

See Also: histogram



box plot
A graph that shows the five-number summary. A box goes from Q1 to Q3, with a line at the median. Lines called whiskers go out to the minimum and the maximum. If there are outliers, a whisker stops at the last value that is not an outlier.
See Also: five-number summary, quartile



categorical data
Data that puts each answer into a group or category, like “bus, car, or walk.” It is not a measurement.
See Also: two-way table



causation
When one thing actually makes another thing happen. A correlation does not prove causation.
See Also: lurking variable



center
A single number that describes a typical value in a data set. The mean and the median are measures of center.
See Also: mean, median, spread



cluster sample
Split the population into groups (clusters). Then randomly choose some whole clusters and use everyone in them.
See Also: stratified sample



combination
A group where order does not matter. The number of ways to choose \(r\) things from \(n\) is \({}_nC_r = \dbinom{n}{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\), read “\(n\) choose \(r\).”
See Also: permutation



complement
The event that \(A\) does not happen. \(P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)\). Some books write \(P(A^C)\).



completely randomized design
An experiment design where chance alone decides which treatment group each subject joins.
See Also: randomized block design, matched pairs



conditional distribution
The percents for one variable inside a single group. Divide each count in that group’s row (or column) by the group’s total.
See Also: marginal distribution, association



conditional probability
The probability of \(A\) when you know \(B\) happened. Written \(P(A \mid B)\) and read “the probability of \(A\) given \(B\).”
\[P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\]



control group
The group in an experiment that does not get the new treatment. It may get a placebo or the usual treatment.
See Also: placebo



convenience sample
A sample of people who are easy to reach. It is usually biased.
See Also: bias



correlation coefficient
A number \(r\) from \(-1\) to \(1\) that measures the direction and strength of a linear pattern. Close to \(1\) or \(-1\) is strong. Close to \(0\) is weak.
See Also: scatterplot, causation



counting principle
If one choice has \(m\) options and a second choice has \(n\) options, there are \(m \cdot n\) ways to make both choices.



data
Facts or numbers that we collect to learn about something.

Example:
The number of pets each student in a class has.




dependent events
Events where one happening changes the probability of the other.

Example:
Drawing two marbles without putting the first one back.

See Also: independent events



distribution
All the values in a data set and how often each one happens. A graph of the data shows its distribution.
See Also: shape



dot plot
A graph that puts one dot above a number line for each data value. Dots for the same value stack up.
See Also: frequency table, histogram



double-blind
An experiment where neither the subjects nor the people measuring the results know who got which treatment.



empirical distribution
A probability distribution made from data. Each probability is a count divided by the total.
See Also: theoretical probability



empirical rule
In a normal distribution, about 68% of the data is within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95% is within 2, and about 99.7% is within 3. Also called the 68-95-99.7 rule.
See Also: normal distribution



expected payoff
The expected value of the net gain. Let \(X\) = the net gain. Then the expected payoff is \(E(X) = \Sigma\, x \cdot P(x)\). A negative expected payoff means you lose money on average.
See Also: expected value, net gain



expected value
The long-run average of a random variable: \(E(X) = \Sigma\, x \cdot P(x)\). Multiply each value by its probability and add. Also called the mean of \(X\), \(\mu_X\).
See Also: expected payoff



experiment
A study where the researcher gives a treatment on purpose and measures what happens. With random assignment, an experiment can show cause and effect.
See Also: treatment, random assignment



experimental probability
A probability found from trials: the number of times an event happened divided by the number of trials.
See Also: law of large numbers



explanatory variable
The variable a researcher changes, or uses to explain changes in another variable. In a scatterplot, it goes on the \(x\)-axis.
See Also: response variable



extrapolation
Using a line to predict far outside the range of the data. Extrapolation is risky and can give answers that make no sense.



factorial
\(n! = n \cdot (n-1) \cdot (n-2) \cdots 2 \cdot 1\), read “\(n\) factorial.” It counts the ways to arrange \(n\) things in order. By definition, \(0! = 1\).

Example:
\(4! = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 24\)




fair
A way of choosing is fair if every person has the same probability of being chosen. A coin is fair if heads and tails each have probability \(\frac{1}{2}\).
See Also: fair game



fair game
A game where the expected value of the money you win or lose is 0. On average, no one wins or loses money.



fence
A cutoff for outliers. The lower fence is \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\). The upper fence is \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\). A value outside the fences is an outlier.
See Also: outlier, interquartile range



five-number summary
Five numbers that describe a data set: the minimum, Q1, the median, Q3, and the maximum.
See Also: box plot, quartile



frequency
How many times a value happens in a data set.

Example:
In the data 2, 3, 3, 5, the value 3 has a frequency of 2.




frequency table
A table that lists each value and its frequency.
See Also: frequency, tally



generalize
To say that results from a sample are true for the whole population. This is only safe when the sample was chosen at random.
See Also: sample, population



histogram
A bar graph for number data. The values are put in groups called bins. The bars touch, and the height of each bar is how many values are in that bin.
See Also: bin, dot plot



independent events
Events where one happening does not change the probability of the other. Then \(P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)\), and \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\).
See Also: dependent events



interquartile range
The distance from Q1 to Q3. It shows how spread out the middle half of the data is. Also called the IQR.
\[\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\]
See Also: quartile, range



intersection
\(A \cap B\), read “\(A\) intersect \(B\)” or “\(A\) and \(B\).” Both \(A\) and \(B\) happen. In a Venn diagram, it is the overlap.
See Also: union, multiplication rule



IQR
Short for interquartile range: \(Q_3 - Q_1\). It shows how spread out the middle half of the data is.
See Also: interquartile range



law of large numbers
As the number of trials grows, the experimental probability usually gets closer to the theoretical probability.



least-squares regression line
The line that makes \(\Sigma(y - \hat{y})^2\), the sum of the squared residuals, as small as possible.
See Also: residual



line of best fit
A line that follows the trend of the dots in a scatterplot. About the same number of dots are above it as below it. Also called a trend line.
See Also: least-squares regression line, y-hat



lurking variable
A hidden variable that affects both variables in a study. It can make two things look connected when one does not cause the other.

Example:
Hot weather causes both more ice cream sales and more sunburns.




marginal distribution
The percents for one variable, found from the totals in the margins of a two-way table. Divide each total by the grand total.
See Also: conditional distribution



matched pairs
An experiment design with pairs. Each subject gets both treatments in a random order. Or very similar subjects are paired, and each one gets a different treatment.



maximum
The largest value in a data set.



mean
Add up all the values. Then divide by how many values there are. Also called the average.
\[\bar{x} = \frac{\Sigma x}{n}\]

Example:
The mean of 2, 3, 8, 3, 4 is \(20 \div 5 = 4\).

See Also: median



median
The middle value when the data is in order. With an even number of values, the median is halfway between the two middle values.

Example:
The median of 2, 3, 3, 4, 8 is 3.

See Also: mean



minimum
The smallest value in a data set.



mode
The value that happens most often in a data set.



mu
The Greek letter \(\mu\), read “mew.” It stands for the mean of a population, of a normal distribution, or of a random variable (\(\mu_X\)).
See Also: x-bar, sigma



multiplication rule
\(P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A)\). For independent events, this is \(P(A) \cdot P(B)\).



mutually exclusive
Events that cannot happen at the same time. Then \(P(A \cap B) = 0\) and \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)\).



n
The number of values in a data set. In \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{\Sigma x}{n}\), you divide by \(n\).
See Also: x-bar, sigma notation



net gain
What you win minus what you paid. It is negative when you lose money.



normal distribution
A bell-shaped, symmetric distribution. Its mean and median are equal and sit in the center. It is described by its mean and its standard deviation.
See Also: empirical rule, z-score



observational study
A study that watches or measures without changing anything. It can show an association but not a cause.
See Also: experiment



outlier
A value that is far away from the rest of the data. A common rule: a value is an outlier if it is more than \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) below Q1 or above Q3.
See Also: fence



percentile
The percent of the data that is below a value.

Example:
A score at the 75th percentile is higher than 75% of the scores.

See Also: z-score, quartile



permutation
An arrangement where order matters. The number of ways to arrange \(r\) things chosen from \(n\) is \({}_nP_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}\), read “\(n\) permute \(r\).”
See Also: combination



placebo
A fake treatment that looks real, like a sugar pill. People can feel better just from believing they were treated (the placebo effect).



population
The whole group we want to learn about.

Example:
All students at a school. A sample might be 50 of those students.

See Also: sample



probability
A number from 0 to 1 that tells how likely something is. 0 means impossible and 1 means certain. \(P(A)\) is read “the probability of \(A\).”
\[P(A) = \frac{\text{number of ways } A \text{ can happen}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}\]



probability distribution
A list or graph of every value of a random variable and its probability. Every probability is from 0 to 1, and they add to 1: \(\Sigma P(x) = 1\).
See Also: random variable, expected value



quartile
The three values that cut ordered data into four parts with the same number of values. Q1 is the median of the lower half. The median is Q2. Q3 is the median of the upper half.
See Also: five-number summary, interquartile range



random assignment
Using chance to decide which subjects get which treatment. It makes the groups alike, so a difference can be blamed on the treatment.
See Also: experiment



random variable
A number that comes from a chance process, such as the number of heads in 3 coin flips. It is often written with a capital letter, like \(X\).
See Also: probability distribution



randomized block design
An experiment design that first splits the subjects into groups that are alike (blocks). Then the treatments are randomly assigned inside each block.
See Also: completely randomized design, matched pairs



range
The maximum minus the minimum. It shows how spread out all the data is.
See Also: interquartile range



relative frequency
A count divided by a total, written as a fraction, decimal, or percent.

Example:
12 out of 60 students is a relative frequency of \(\frac{12}{60} = 20\%\).

See Also: frequency, two-way table



replication
Using many subjects in an experiment. With more subjects, chance differences between the groups get smaller.
See Also: experiment, random assignment



residual
The actual value minus the predicted value: \(y - \hat{y}\). A positive residual means the point is above the line.
See Also: residual plot, least-squares regression line



residual plot
A graph of the residuals against \(x\). Random scatter means a line is a good model. A pattern, like a curve, means it is not.
See Also: residual



response variable
The variable that is measured to see the effect. In a scatterplot, it goes on the \(y\)-axis.
See Also: explanatory variable



sample
A part of a group that we collect data from. We use the sample to learn about the whole group (the population).
See Also: population



sample survey
A study that asks a sample of people questions.
See Also: observational study, experiment



scatterplot
A graph of two numbers for each person or thing. Each dot shows one pair \((x, y)\).
See Also: line of best fit, correlation coefficient



segmented bar chart
A bar chart where each bar is 100% of one group, split into parts. It shows conditional distributions side by side.
See Also: conditional distribution



shape
What a graph of the data looks like: symmetric, skewed left, or skewed right.
See Also: symmetric, skewed left, skewed right



sigma
The small Greek letter \(\sigma\). It stands for the standard deviation of a population or of a normal distribution. The capital letter \(\Sigma\) means something different: add up.
See Also: standard deviation, mu



simple random sample
A sample where every group of people of that size has the same chance of being chosen. Also called an SRS.
See Also: stratified sample



simulation
Using random numbers or shuffling to copy a chance process many times, to see what usually happens.
See Also: statistically significant



skewed left
A shape where most values are high and a long tail stretches to the left. The mean is less than the median.
See Also: skewed right, tail



skewed right
A shape where most values are low and a long tail stretches to the right. The mean is greater than the median.

Example:
US household income is skewed right.

See Also: skewed left, tail



slope
How much \(y\) changes when \(x\) goes up by 1. For a line of best fit, when \(x\) goes up by 1, the predicted \(y\) changes by the slope.
See Also: y-intercept



spread
How far apart the values in a data set are. The range, the IQR, and the standard deviation are measures of spread.
See Also: range, interquartile range, standard deviation



standard deviation
A number that tells how far the values in a data set usually are from the mean. A small standard deviation means the values are close to the mean. It is often written \(s\) (for a sample) or SD.
\[s = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma(x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}\]
See Also: variance, mean



statistically significant
A result that would rarely happen by chance alone. Usually this means less than 5% of the time.
See Also: simulation



stratified sample
Split the population into groups that are alike (strata). Then take a random sample from each group.
See Also: cluster sample



symmetric
A shape where the left side and the right side look about the same. The mean and the median are about equal.



systematic sample
Pick a random starting point. Then choose every \(k\)th person on a list.



tail
The long, low side of a graph. The mean is pulled toward the tail.



tally
A mark made for each data value as you count it.



theoretical distribution
A probability distribution found by reasoning about the chance process (equally likely outcomes, or the multiplication rule), not from data.
See Also: empirical distribution, probability distribution



theoretical probability
A probability found by reasoning about equally likely outcomes.
See Also: experimental probability



treatment
What the researcher does to the subjects in an experiment.
See Also: experiment, control group



tree diagram
A diagram with branches that shows each stage of a chance process. Multiply along a path to find the probability of that path.



trial
One run of a chance process, such as one flip of a coin or one set of 3 free throws in a simulation.



two-way table
A table that shows counts for two categorical variables at once. The groups of one variable name the rows. The groups of the other variable name the columns. The totals are in the margins.
See Also: relative frequency, venn diagram



union
\(A \cup B\), read “\(A\) union \(B\)” or “\(A\) or \(B\).” \(A\) happens, \(B\) happens, or both happen.
See Also: intersection, addition rule



variance
The standard deviation squared. To find it, add the squared differences from the mean and divide by \(n - 1\).
See Also: standard deviation



Venn diagram
A picture that uses overlapping circles to show groups. The overlap shows what is in both groups. The space outside the circles shows what is in neither.
See Also: two-way table



whisker
A line on a box plot that goes from the box out to the smallest or largest value that is not an outlier.
See Also: box plot



with replacement
Each item is put back before the next draw. Every draw has the same probabilities, so the draws are independent.
See Also: without replacement, independent events



without replacement
Each item stays out after it is drawn. The probabilities change from one draw to the next, so the draws are dependent.
See Also: with replacement, dependent events



x-bar
The symbol \(\bar{x}\), read “x-bar.” It stands for the mean of a sample: \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{\Sigma x}{n}\).
See Also: mean, mu



y-hat
The symbol \(\hat{y}\), read “y-hat.” It stands for a predicted value of \(y\) from a line, such as \(\hat{y} = 5x + 54\).
See Also: residual



y-intercept
The value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\). For a line of best fit, it is the predicted \(y\) when \(x = 0\). Sometimes it has no real meaning.
See Also: slope



z-score
How many standard deviations a value is above or below the mean. A positive z-score is above the mean. A negative z-score is below the mean.
\[z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\]
See Also: standard deviation, percentile



z-table
A table that gives the area under the standard normal curve to the left of a z-score. That area is the proportion of the data below the z-score.
See Also: z-score, normal distribution



Σ (sigma notation)
\(\Sigma\) is the Greek capital letter sigma. In statistics it means add up.

Example:
For the data 2, 3, 5: \(\Sigma x = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10\).

See Also: x-bar, mean
